readerTitle: Camp David: when both sides can get what they really want
caseNote: 실제 사건 (1978년 캠프 데이비드 협상, 이집트·이스라엘 시나이 반도 문제) + 가상 적용 (B2B 컨설팅, 가구 제조사와 운송사)
insight: 요구가 정면으로 부딪혀도 그 요구를 만든 이유는 부딪히지 않을 수 있다. 막힌 협상에서는 선을 어디에 그을지보다 각자 왜 원하는지를 먼저 묻는다.
misconception: 양쪽 요구가 정반대라면 중간에서 나누거나 한쪽이 양보하는 것 말고는 답이 없다.

sources.text: Fisher, R. & Ury, W. (1981). Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In. 시나이 반도의 주권 대 안보 사례
U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian: Camp David Accords and the Arab-Israeli Peace Process, 1977–1980
Jimmy Carter Presidential Library: The Camp David Accords (1978년 9월 회담 일정과 참가자)
Treaty of Peace between the Arab Republic of Egypt and the State of Israel (1979), 부속서의 병력 제한 구역 조항
Multinational Force and Observers (MFO): 시나이 국제 감시단 설립 배경
Wright, L. (2014). Thirteen Days in September. 회담 경과 참고

factChecks.note: 회담 기간 '13일'(1978년 9월 5~17일)은 Carter Library와 State Department 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
이스라엘이 1967년 전쟁 이후 시나이를 점령했다는 점, 1979년 평화조약 서명, 1982년 철수 완료는 Office of the Historian 자료로 확인하세요.
주권(이집트) 대 안보(이스라엘) 구도와 비무장화 해법은 Getting to Yes 1장의 설명을 따랐습니다. 실제 협상은 이보다 복잡했고, 카드는 단순화한 설명입니다.
5번 카드의 '국경 근처 이집트 병력 제한'과 '국제 감시단'은 조약 부속서와 MFO 자료로 확인하세요. 감시단(MFO)은 1981년에 꾸려졌으므로 카드에서는 시점을 따로 적지 않았습니다.
팔레스타인 자치 틀이 대부분 이행되지 않았고 팔레스타인 대표가 회담에 참석하지 않았다는 점은 State Department 자료로 확인하세요.
6번과 8번 카드(컨설팅, 가구 제조사·운송사)는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치(10%)도 가상입니다.

cards.title: Camp David: when both sides can get what they really want
body: In September 1978, US President Jimmy Carter hosted Egypt's Anwar Sadat and Israel's Menachem Begin at Camp David, the presidential retreat outside Washington. They stayed for thirteen days.
One of the hardest issues was the Sinai Peninsula, a desert Israel had held since the 1967 war. Each side's demand seemed to rule out the other's.

image.label: Two chairs facing each other across a desert map
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 숲속 오두막 안 탁자 위에 사막 지도가 펼쳐져 있고, 양쪽에 빈 의자 두 개가 마주 봄. 실존 인물의 얼굴, 국기, 정부 문장은 넣지 않음.

cards.title: You're the mediator.
body: Egypt insists on getting all of the Sinai back. Israel insists on keeping part of it. Every map you draw, one side rejects.

options.text: Propose splitting the land roughly in half
options.feedback: It looks fair and it's quick. But any line leaves Egypt short of what it said it must have, and it may not give Israel what it actually needs either.

options.text: Ask each side why it wants what it's demanding
options.feedback: It takes time and trust, but it can show you that two clashing demands come from needs that don't clash. That's what this lesson is about.

options.text: Offer each side outside rewards to give ground
options.feedback: Sweeteners can help close a deal. But they don't touch the core conflict over the land, so the deadlock stays.

cards.title: Same desert, different needs.
body: Egypt's demand came from **sovereignty**. The Sinai was Egyptian land. Giving up any of it was a matter of national honor that no Egyptian leader could accept.
Israel's demand came from **security**. It did not want Egyptian tanks and troops able to gather close to its border again.
Stated as demands, the two were opposites. Stated as needs, they were about different things.

cards.title: Interests behind positions
body: A **position** is what someone says they want. An **interest** is why they want it.

Roger Fisher and William Ury used the Sinai as a central example in their 1981 book *Getting to Yes*. Their point: positions can be impossible to reconcile while the interests behind them fit together. Bargaining over positions only moves a line. Working on interests can change the shape of the deal.

image.label: Two icebergs: small tips labeled demands, large bases labeled reasons
image.brief: 빙산 두 개 인포그래픽. 물 위의 작은 끝에는 "Position: all of it", "Position: part of it". 물 아래의 큰 몸통에는 "Interest: sovereignty", "Interest: security". 물 아래 몸통이 서로 겹치지 않고 나란히 들어맞는 모양.

cards.title: The whole Sinai went back, without the armies.
body: The agreements returned all of the Sinai to Egypt. In return, large areas were demilitarized, with limits on Egyptian forces near Israel's border and international observers to check them.

Egypt got its flag back over its land. Israel got a buffer that kept armies away. The peace treaty was signed in 1979, and Israel finished withdrawing in 1982. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize.

image.label: Map of a peninsula with shaded zones of limited forces
image.brief: 단순화한 반도 지도. 전체가 한 가지 색(돌려받은 땅)으로 칠해져 있고, 국경 쪽으로 갈수록 옅어지는 줄무늬 구역 "Limited forces" 표시와 작은 망원경 아이콘 "Observers". 국기와 실제 지명 표기는 생략.

cards.title: It works in a client meeting too.
body: A client tells a consulting firm: "Fixed fee only." The firm says: "Hourly only." Stuck.

Ask why. The client needs a number its finance team can approve. The firm fears the project growing with no extra pay. A fixed fee for a clearly defined scope, with priced change requests for anything extra, meets both interests.
cards.softwareNote: A customer demanding a 30% discount may really need the purchase to fit under a budget limit this year. A smaller first year that grows with usage can meet that need without cutting your price.

cards.title: Not every clash hides a fit.
body: Camp David also produced a framework for Palestinian self-government. Much of it was never carried out. The interests there conflicted more deeply, and Palestinian representatives were not at the table.

Looking for interests also needs trust. People share their real reasons only when they believe you won't use them against them. Sometimes the interests truly collide, and then your alternatives and walk-away point matter most.

cards.title: Now it's a trucking contract.
body: A furniture maker tells its carrier: cut rates 10% or we switch. The carrier can't go that low without losing money.
The carrier asks why. The maker's real problem is rising cost per delivered order, driven by damaged goods and missed delivery windows that its retailers charge penalties for.

options.text: Match the 10% cut to keep the account
options.feedback: You keep the customer but lose money on every load, and the damage and penalty problem is still there.

options.text: Keep the rate, but offer better packing and guaranteed delivery windows that cut the maker's penalties
options.feedback: This works on the maker's interest, total cost, not its position, a lower rate. Both sides can come out ahead.

options.text: Hold the rate and assume the maker is bluffing
options.feedback: Holding firm protects your margin. But you're still arguing over the position and could lose the account over a problem you could solve.

cards.title: When demands clash, look at the reasons behind them.
body: Two opposite demands can come from needs that fit together. Find the needs, then design a deal around them.
**Try it today:** pick one stuck negotiation. Write down each side's demand, then one reason behind it. Look for a deal that meets both reasons.
